newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin shuns NATO's expansion summit in Madrid.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin shuns NATO's expansion summit in Madrid.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin said on Thursday he would not go to the July summit of NATO states that is expected to invite some east European countries to join because Russians would be uncomfortable with his presence there.
Itar-Tass news agency quoted Yeltsin as saying a special group of advisers considered whether he should go to the Madrid meeting.

"We have decided that we need a little pause after the signing of the Founding Act (on relations between NATO and Russia)," it quoted him as telling a group of journalists from the Group of Seven leading industrial democracies.
"The Russians would not feel comfortable," Yeltsin added in a clear reference to wide domestic opposition to NATO expansion.
Yeltsin had not been expected to attend the Madrid summit, but some speculation both in Moscow and in the West indicated the 66-year-old Kremlin leader might change his mind.

Tass quoted him as saying his decision "should not result in negative consequences in Russia's relations with other states". A Kremlin press statement had earlier announced Yeltsin's decision not to travel to Madrid.

Russia is opposed to the Western alliance's eastward expansion, saying the move would harm its security interests and push Russia out of Europe. But Moscow has not closed the door completely despite its reservations.

The Russian leader's communist and nationalist opponents have accused him of selling out to the West, which plans to expand the NATO defence alliance to take in some of Moscow's former communist allies despite fierce Russian opposition.

Russia's former communist allies Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary are expected to be admitted to NATO in the first round. Romania and Slovenia are also fighting for quick membership but face U.S. resistance.
Moscow tacitly accepted the first round in exchange for some Western security pledges and signed a cooperation pact with the alliance in May in Paris.
But it still firmly opposes NATO membership for former Soviet republics such as the Baltic states or Ukraine.
Later on Thursday, Yeltsin leaves Moscow for the United States, where he is due to take part in a summit in Denver with the leaders of the Group of Seven.
